sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Nucleotide Transformer v2 represents DNA using an encoder pretrained on multiple species. Encoder-only transformer with 6-mer tokenization, rotary position embeddings and SwiGLU feed-forward layers. The documented inputs are DNA sequences with tokenization determined by 6-mers and individual ambiguous/remainder bases. The output consists of contextual DNA embeddings and masked-token probabilities; downstream tasks need adaptation.

record.name: Choose a DNA sequence model for genomic element annotation
record.description: Which DNA sequence model, and which way of using it, classifies genomic elements such as promoters, enhancers, splice sites and histone marks most accurately for my sequences?

attributes.question: Which DNA sequence model, and which way of using it, classifies genomic elements such as promoters, enhancers, splice sites and histone marks most accurately for my sequences?
intended_users: Researchers choosing a DNA sequence model to annotate or classify regions of a genome
Method developers comparing a new DNA sequence model with published ones
attributes.decision: Choose a DNA sequence model, and whether to probe its frozen embeddings or fine-tune it, for a sequence annotation task.
inputs: DNA sequences of the element type of interest, with genome build and species
Labelled examples, or none if only a frozen probe is planned
A compute budget, which decides whether fine-tuning is possible
attributes.output: Per-task scores for each model under each training regime, with the task's split, kept separate by benchmark.
attributes.setting: Research genome annotation from sequence. Short-range and long-range tasks, frozen probes and fine-tuning are separate comparisons; a rank on one does not transfer to another.
exclusions: Variant effect prediction, which has its own use cases for missense, regulatory, rare-disease and splicing variants
Sequence conservation scores and synthetic promoter expression level, which are not element annotation
Pooling scores across benchmarks: each runs its own models, splits and probes
Gene expression level, three-dimensional genome structure, and classifying a sequence's species or viral lineage, which answer other questions
attributes.clinical_scope: Research only. Nothing recorded here supports a clinical or diagnostic decision.
evidence_gaps: The evidence comes from four studies: GenBench, SegmentNT, the Nucleotide Transformer benchmark and GUANinE v1.1. GUANinE contributes only two regression tasks. The models they cover overlap only partly, so a model ranked well in one may be missing from the others.

Simple comparators are in the evidence (GUANinE's 5-mer and GC-content baselines, GenBench's CNN, a raw-sequence probe in the Nucleotide Transformer benchmark), but none has been named as the baseline these models must beat.
GENEB's results are not used yet: each model's score mixes element categories with species and virus classification and with averages over all tasks, and the categories have to be separated first.

BEND, DART-Eval and Gene-MTEB results cannot be used yet: their scored results have not passed review or are recorded in a form that cannot be linked. BEND's reviewed tests are variant effect tasks, which this page excludes.
Automated source review only. No human scientific review, and nothing here was reproduced.

record.name: Rank close analogues of a hit by binding affinity
record.description: Which method ranks a hit's close analogues by binding affinity accurately enough to choose what to make next, and at what compute cost against free energy calculation?

attributes.question: Which method ranks a hit's close analogues by binding affinity accurately enough to choose what to make next, and at what compute cost against free energy calculation?
intended_users: Medicinal chemists choosing which analogues of a confirmed hit to synthesise next
Computational chemists deciding whether to spend free energy calculation on a series
Project leads budgeting compute against synthesis in a lead-optimisation campaign
attributes.decision: Choose which analogues of a confirmed hit to make next, and choose the method and compute budget used to rank them.
inputs: A confirmed hit and a set of close analogues, with the series' chemical relationship stated
A protein structure or sequence for the target, and its relationship to any structure used in training
Measured affinities for part of the series, with the assay type and units recorded
An available compute budget and a synthesis budget
attributes.output: A ranking of the analogues by predicted binding affinity, with an error estimate against measured affinities on comparable series, the leakage control that estimate rests on, and the compute cost of producing it.
attributes.setting: Research-stage lead optimisation within one target's congeneric series. Ranking across unrelated targets, hit discovery from a large library and absolute affinity prediction are separate questions.
exclusions: Most extracted numbers are averages across series, which do not say how well a given series would be ranked. The leakage-controlled CASP16 tests are the exception: each scores one congeneric series (L1000, chymase; L3000, autotaxin).
A correlation pooled or averaged over unrelated targets does not answer this question and flatters every method.
Accuracy on a benchmark series does not establish that a chosen analogue will be more potent, nor that it will be developable.
IC50, Ki and Kd are not interchangeable; sources that convert between them do so under a stated assumption that must be carried with the number.
Compute-cost comparisons are only meaningful against a measured alternative. The extracted tables print no measured cost for FEP+.
attributes.clinical_scope: Research only. Affinity ranking does not establish efficacy, safety or clinical suitability.
evidence_gaps: Automated source review only; independent human scientific review remains outstanding.

No reviewed source in the store publishes per-series affinity-ranking values for any machine-learning method. Every value recorded for a machine-learning method is a mean over series, so the question 'would this method have ranked my series correctly' cannot be answered from the store, only 'on average across these series'.

Per-series values are recoverable for the baselines but not for the machine-learning arms. The public_binding_free_energy_benchmark repository (MIT, releases v1.0 and v2.0) holds FEP+ per-edge results and the OpenFE per-transformation deposits on Zenodo cover the OpenFE arm; nothing was computed from either in this pass. The Boltz repository publishes no affinity predictions: at commit b1ebfc46ecf57f5414e0d1a6f9027bbb122c53bc its README and docs/evaluation.md still list the FEP+, CASP16 and MF-PCBA affinity predictions and the Boltz-2 evaluation scripts as 'coming soon'.
A comparison must not mix the two granularities: published per-series FEP+ values cannot be set beside Boltz-2's series averages in one comparison.

No fully independent evaluation of a machine-learning affinity predictor against free energy calculation on the same measured congeneric series was found. Both same-series comparisons that exist are reported by the developers of the machine-learning method, and both take their FEP+ arm from a benchmark whose protocol was tuned per system after seeing the error against experiment.

The peer-reviewed OpenFE industry benchmark (doi 10.1021/acs.jcim.6c00089) is behind an ACS paywall and was not retrieved, so the open-source free energy arm rests on a blog post the Boltz-2 supplement cites.
No measured compute cost for FEP+ exists in any extracted table; the only cost column prints '-' for FEP+ and ranges for OpenFE and ABFE.
No uncertainty is printed for any Boltz-2 supplement cell; the bootstrap error bars are figure-only.
The CASP16 assessors' per-group and per-target Kendall tau values are figure-only and were not extracted; the official per-target results file was not downloaded.

Neither the Merck FEP benchmark (Schindler et al. 2020) nor the Hahn et al. 2022 benchmark-construction paper nor the Wu et al. 2025 ABFE protocol paper was retrieved, so the series definitions behind the four-target subset are not established.

MM/GBSA and docking-score comparators on congeneric series were not searched for beyond the arms the Boltz-2 supplement chose for itself; recent affinity models other than Boltz-2, GAT and BACPI were not covered.
The overlap between the 876-complex OpenFE subset and the 87-compound four-target subset is not stated in any source, so the two comparisons cannot be treated as independent.

record.name: Use calibrated computational evidence for missense variants (PP3/BP4)
record.description: Which predictor and score thresholds give calibrated ACMG/AMP computational evidence (PP3/BP4) for a missense variant in a gene without a gene-specific calibration, and at what strength?

attributes.question: Which predictor and score thresholds give calibrated ACMG/AMP computational evidence (PP3/BP4) for a missense variant in a gene without a gene-specific calibration, and at what strength?
intended_users: Clinical scientists classifying germline variants under ACMG/AMP criteria
Variant curation expert panels deciding whether to adopt or replace genome-wide thresholds
attributes.decision: Choose one predictor in advance and the score thresholds at which it supplies PP3 or BP4 evidence at Supporting, Moderate or Strong strength, for a missense variant in a gene with no gene-specific calibration.
inputs: A germline missense variant on a stated transcript and genome build
The chosen predictor's precomputed score at a pinned version
Whether a gene- or region-specific specification exists that supersedes genome-wide thresholds
attributes.output: Calibrated score intervals for each evidence strength per predictor, the highest strength each reaches, the calibration data and its limits, and independent rankings of the same predictors. No variant classification.
attributes.setting: Germline missense variants assessed under ACMG/AMP criteria. The genome-wide calibrations use ClinVar pathogenic and benign missense variants rare in gnomAD, from genes with at least one pathogenic variant, with tools' training variants removed where available, and a prior probability of pathogenicity of 4.41% estimated from gnomAD.
exclusions: Genes with an expert-panel specification that sets its own thresholds (BRCA1/BRCA2 is a separate use case)
Splicing, in-frame indel, protein-truncating and non-coding variants
Combining several predictors, or counting PP3 together with overlapping evidence such as PM1 or allele frequency beyond the recommended caps
Somatic variant oncogenicity
Final variant classification or patient management
attributes.clinical_scope: Clinical research on the evidence strength of computational predictions. Calibrated thresholds hold on average across genes; they do not classify a variant and do not replace expert review.
evidence_gaps: The four tools that reach PP3_Strong in Pejaver et al. 2022 (BayesDel, MutPred2, REVEL, VEST4) each have a developer among that paper's authors; no independent recalibration of them is in the store.
The calibrations are genome-wide; Tejura et al. 2024 show that gene-level performance of REVEL and BayesDel often departs from them. No gene-level calibration is extracted.

Thirteen predictors have four-level intervals (Pejaver et al. 2022) and seven have points-scale intervals (Bergquist et al. 2025). Newer predictors ranked highly by Livesey and Marsh 2025 (for example popEVE, CPT-1) have no ClinGen calibration in the store.
Pejaver et al. 2022 Table S1 (point estimates and one-sided confidence bounds) was not retrieved.

A 2026 Genetics in Medicine calibration of machine-learning predictors (doi:10.1016/j.gim.2026.102606) is closed access and was not retrieved; the BayesQuantify (J Med Genet 2025) and P-KNN (bioRxiv 2025) joint calibrations were found but not extracted.
Evidence yield in real genomes (Stenton et al. 2024 Table 2) and reclassification impact (Dubé et al. 2026, Genet Med Open) were found but not extracted.
The Livesey and Marsh and ProteinGym rankings measure discrimination, not calibrated evidence strength; they help choose which predictors to calibrate, not which thresholds to apply.
Qualified human scientific review is outstanding; automated transcription does not establish replication.

record.description: Which DNA/RNA evidence workflow identifies splice-altering variants for inherited-disorder follow-up when patient RNA and tissue-specific context are available?

attributes.question: Which DNA/RNA evidence workflow identifies splice-altering variants for inherited-disorder follow-up when patient RNA and tissue-specific context are available?
intended_users: Clinical researchers scoping the available diagnostic-genomics evidence
Computational researchers comparing exact evaluated configurations
attributes.decision: Inspect the FRASER known pathogenic-event recovery curve and the sequence-classification proxy evidence before selecting a workflow and designing patient-RNA follow-up for the intended cohort size.
inputs: Patient skin-fibroblast (or matched tissue) RNA-seq aligned reads
The number of samples available for a FRASER-style aberrant-splicing cohort
attributes.output: A sourced recovery curve (fraction of known pathogenic splicing events recovered as cohort size grows) and a separate sequence-classification proxy; no diagnostic-yield claim for unknown cases.
attributes.setting: FRASER, applied to a retrospective Kremer rare-mitochondrial-disorder skin-fibroblast RNA cohort (119 samples/105 individuals, 13 known pathogenic splicing events), recovers a mean 85% (11 of 13) of known events at a reduced 30-sample subsample. Separate, proxy sequence-classification results for DNA foundation models (Alavi et al. 2026: Evo 2 40B, Genos 10B and NTv3 650M classifying variants with established splicing defects against benign variants) are also linked, scoped as a different endpoint. Feng et al. 2025 Table 1 splice acceptor and donor classification is linked to 'Prioritise variants for splicing experiments', not here.
exclusions: Diagnostic yield in patients without a known pathogenic event (this is recovery of already-known events, not discovery)
Full-cohort outlier-gene workload counts (12/7/10 genes/sample), a different population from the 30-sample recovery evaluation and not ingested here
Blinded pathogenicity adjudication or VUS reclassification
attributes.clinical_scope: Clinical applicability is not established beyond known-event recovery. This does not demonstrate prospective diagnostic yield, blinded adjudication, or general tissue transfer.
evidence_gaps: No numeric confidence interval is reported for the 85% recovery figure in the inspected main text.
Subsampling repeat count and exact score-aggregation method are unextracted.

Feng et al. 2025 Table 1 splice-site classification is not linked to this use case: it measures AUC on benchmark splice-site sequences (DNABERT-2/NT datasets), not patient RNA, and is linked to 'Prioritise variants for splicing experiments'. The DNA foundation-model results linked here (Alavi et al. 2026: Evo 2 40B, Genos 10B and NTv3 650M) are threshold classifications of variants with established splicing defects, also proxies; none recovers events from patient RNA-seq.
